steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper Sieve, a method for pruning noisy web-crawled image-text datasets for CLIP pretraining using an image-captioning model. Explain why data quality matters for CLIP, the limits of existing pruning methods like CLIPScore, how our approach works, and the headline DataComp results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- CLIP and why its representation quality matters for VLMs
- Noisy web-crawled pretraining data
- Existing data pruning methods and their limits
- CLIPScore: false positives and false negatives
- Our approach (Sieve) and DataComp results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- CLIP (cite)
  - success in zero-shot image classification, multimodal retrieval
  - pretrained CLIP encoders used in VLMs: conditioning image generation on CLIP text embeddings (cite), retrieval augmented VLMs (cite), aligning audio/depth/thermal with language via CLIP image embeddings (cite)
  - -> CLIP representation quality influences many VLMs
- Pretraining data
  - billions of image-text pairs from common crawl
  - diverse but noisy: low quality images, low quality alt-text, misaligned pairs
  - noisy data hurts learned representations, poor downstream performance (cite)
- Existing pruning
  - heuristics: image dimensions, aspect ratio, alt-text length, complexity (cite); reduce noise but can limit diversity (cite)
  - using images/class names from datasets like ImageNet to sample similar pairs: higher downstream accuracy (cite), but limited diversity (close to one dataset)
- CLIPScore (cite)
  - cosine similarity of image/text embeddings from pretrained CLIP; rank alignment
  - false positives (Figure 1): poorly aligned but high score (bad samples), spurious correlations of pretrained CLIP (cite)
  - false negatives: aligned but low score (hard samples), poor discrimination hard vs bad
  - excluding hard + including bad hurts generalization of encoders
- Sieve
  - goal: reduce false negatives/positives via image-captioning model pretrained on small, diverse, well-aligned pairs
  - Figure 1: helps where CLIPScore focuses on geographic/chronological context rather than content
  - Figure 2: multiple captions per image with nucleus sampling (cite); remove medium phrases ("an image of", "a photo of")
  - lightweight sentence transformer (pretrained on unlabeled text) embeds captions vs alt-text; alignment = proxy for image-text alignment; fuse with CLIPScore
  - DataComp (cite): fixed CLIP hyperparameters, candidate pools; select subset for best performance on 38 downstream tasks
  - results: +2.6% / +1.7% over CLIPScore on average of 38 tasks (medium / large pool); retrieval +2.7% / +4.5%

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models have been very successful at zero-shot image classification and multimodal retrieval tasks. Also, many foundational Vision-Language Models (VLMs) use pretrained CLIP encoders, to condition image generation on CLIP text embeddings, in retrieval augmented vision-language models, and to align modalities like audio, depth, and thermal with language through CLIP image embeddings. So the quality of CLIP representations can affect the performance of many VLMs.

To pretrain CLIP, billions of image-text pairs are collected with common crawl. This raw data is very diverse, but it has many noisy image-text pairs, including low quality images, low quality alternative text (alt-text), and image-text pairs that are misaligned. Pretraining CLIP models on noisy data can hurt the learned representations, and this leads to bad performance on downstream tasks.

To deal with this problem, researchers have developed data pruning methods that remove low quality image-text pairs. Heuristics that filter out image-text pairs based on image dimensions, aspect ratio, alt-text length, and complexity are commonly used to reduce noise, but they can also limit the diversity of the dataset. Methods that use images or class names from datasets like ImageNet to sample image-text pairs that are semantically similar can give higher accuracy on downstream tasks, but they limit the diversity of the selected samples, because they sample image-text pairs that are close to one specific dataset.

- CLIPScore: cosine similarity of image and text embeddings from pretrained CLIP, used to rank alignment
  - false positives (Figure 1): bad samples with high score, from spurious correlations
  - false negatives: hard samples with low score
  - hurts generalization of encoders
- Our method:
  - image-captioning model pretrained on small, diverse, well-aligned pairs
  - Figure 1: cases where CLIPScore looks at geographic/chronological context
  - Figure 2: multiple captions via nucleus sampling, remove medium phrases ("an image of", "a photo of"), sentence transformer embedding, alignment with alt-text as proxy, fused with CLIPScore
  - DataComp: 38 downstream tasks; +2.6% and +1.7% (medium/large); retrieval +2.7% and +4.5%

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models have been very successful at zero-shot image classification and multimodal retrieval tasks. Also, many foundational Vision-Language Models (VLMs) use pretrained CLIP encoders, to condition image generation on CLIP text embeddings, in retrieval augmented vision-language models, and to align modalities like audio, depth, and thermal with language through CLIP image embeddings. So the quality of CLIP representations can affect the performance of many VLMs.

To pretrain CLIP, billions of image-text pairs are collected with common crawl. This raw data is very diverse, but it has many noisy image-text pairs, including low quality images, low quality alternative text (alt-text), and image-text pairs that are misaligned. Pretraining CLIP models on noisy data can hurt the learned representations, and this leads to bad performance on downstream tasks.

To deal with this problem, researchers have developed data pruning methods that remove low quality image-text pairs. Heuristics that filter out image-text pairs based on image dimensions, aspect ratio, alt-text length, and complexity are commonly used to reduce noise, but they can also limit the diversity of the dataset. Methods that use images or class names from datasets like ImageNet to sample image-text pairs that are semantically similar can give higher accuracy on downstream tasks, but they limit the diversity of the selected samples, because they sample image-text pairs that are close to one specific dataset.

CLIPScore is one of the most effective pruning methods. It computes the cosine similarity between the image and text embeddings with a pretrained CLIP model, and this score is then used to rank how well image-text pairs are aligned. But as Figure 1 shows, CLIPScore can give false positives, which are samples that are poorly aligned but have a high CLIPScore (i.e., bad samples), because of spurious correlations that the pretrained CLIP model learned. CLIPScore can also give false negatives, which are samples that are aligned but have a low CLIPScore (i.e., hard samples), because it does not discriminate well between hard and bad samples. Leaving out hard samples and keeping bad samples can hurt the generalization of the CLIP image and text encoders.

In this work, our goal is to reduce both the false negatives and the false positives that come from CLIPScore ranking, by using an image-captioning model that was pretrained on small, diverse, and well-aligned image-text pairs. Figure 1 shows that Sieve can reduce false positives or false negatives in different scenarios, for example samples where CLIPScore focuses on the geographic or chronological context of an image instead of the content of the image. As Figure 2 shows, we evaluate the alignment of web-crawled image-text pairs like this. First we generate multiple captions for each image using nucleus sampling. Then we remove phrases that describe the medium (e.g., "an image of", "a photo of") and not visual concepts. Finally, to evaluate the semantic similarity between the generated captions, which have limited diversity, and the alt-text, which is very diverse, we use the embedding space of a lightweight sentence transformer that was pretrained on an unlabeled text corpus. The alignment between the generated captions and the alt-text is then used as a proxy for the image-text alignment. We want to fuse this alignment signal with CLIPScore to minimize false positives and negatives, which gives a more aligned pretraining dataset. To evaluate how effective our pruning method is, we use the DataComp benchmark, which fixes the pretraining hyperparameters of CLIP and gives multiple candidate pools of noisy image-text data for pretraining CLIP models. The goal is to pick a subset of the noisy image-text data that gives the best performance on 38 downstream tasks. With image-captioning model alignment scores fused with CLIPScore, we do better than CLIPScore filtering by 2.6% and 1.7% on the average of 38 downstream tasks on the medium and large scale pool respectively. Also, on multimodal retrieval tasks, our approach improves by 2.7% and 4.5% on medium and large scale respectively.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) [1] models have shown great success in zero-shot image classification and multimodal retrieval tasks. In addition, many foundational Vision-Language Models (VLMs) use pretrained CLIP encoders to condition image generation on CLIP text embeddings [2], in retrieval augmented vision-language models [3,4], and to align modalities including audio, depth, and thermal with language through CLIP image embeddings [5]. Therefore, the quality of CLIP representations can influence the performance of many VLMs.

To pretrain CLIP, billions of image-text pairs are collected using common crawl. The raw data is highly diverse but contains many noisy image-text pairs, including low quality images, low quality alternative text (alt-text), and misaligned image-text pairs. Pretraining CLIP models on noisy data can have adverse effects on the learned representations, leading to poor performance on downstream tasks [6].

To address this challenge, researchers have developed data pruning methods that remove low quality image-text pairs. Heuristics that filter out image-text pairs based on image dimensions, aspect ratio, alt-text length, and complexity are commonly used [7,8] to reduce noise, but they can also limit the diversity of the dataset [9]. Methods that use images or class names from datasets such as ImageNet to sample semantically similar image-text pairs can lead to higher accuracy on downstream tasks [10], but they limit the diversity of the selected samples since they sample image-text pairs close to a specific dataset.

One of the most effective pruning methods, CLIPScore [11,7], computes the cosine similarity between image and text embeddings using a pretrained CLIP model, and this score is then used to rank the alignment of image-text pairs. However, as shown in Figure 1, CLIPScore can lead to false positives – samples that are poorly aligned but have a high CLIPScore (i.e., bad samples) – due to spurious correlations learned by the pretrained CLIP model [12]. CLIPScore can also lead to false negatives – samples that are aligned but have a low CLIPScore (i.e., hard samples) – due to poor discrimination between hard and bad samples. Excluding hard samples and including bad samples can negatively affect the generalization of the CLIP image and text encoders.

The goal of this work is to reduce both the false negatives and the false positives induced by CLIPScore ranking by relying on an image-captioning model pretrained on small, diverse, and well-aligned image-text pairs. As shown in Figure 1, Sieve can reduce false positives or false negatives in different scenarios, such as samples where CLIPScore focuses on the geographic or chronological context of an image rather than its content. As depicted in Figure 2, we evaluate the alignment of web-crawled image-text pairs by first generating multiple captions for each image using nucleus sampling [13], and then removing phrases that describe the medium (e.g., "an image of", "a photo of") rather than visual concepts. Finally, to evaluate the semantic similarity between the generated captions, which have limited diversity, and the highly diverse alt-text, we use the embedding space of a lightweight sentence transformer pretrained on an unlabeled text corpus. The alignment between the generated captions and the alt-text then serves as a proxy for image-text alignment. We fuse this alignment signal with CLIPScore to minimize false positives and negatives, leading to a more aligned pretraining dataset. To evaluate the effectiveness of our pruning method, we use the DataComp [8] benchmark, which fixes the pretraining hyperparameters of CLIP and provides multiple candidate pools of noisy image-text data for pretraining CLIP models. The goal is to select the subset of noisy image-text data that leads to the best performance on 38 downstream tasks. Using image-captioning model alignment scores fused with CLIPScore, we surpass CLIPScore filtering by 2.6% and 1.7% on the average of 38 downstream tasks on the medium and large scale pools respectively. In addition, on multimodal retrieval tasks, our approach improves by 2.7% and 4.5% on medium and large scale respectively.
